title: What's Woodenization All About?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares three teacher-generated one-sentence definitions of 'Woodenization' — his term, borrowed from coach John Wooden's practice of teaching college athletes how to put on their socks and shoes, for explicitly and specifically teaching students how to do even seemingly obvious tasks. The definitions come from a professional development session led by PD facilitator Ashley Yazarlou, and Stuart uses each one as a jumping-off point to unpack a different facet of the concept: Ann Marie's definition highlights that no task is too small or obvious to warrant explicit teaching; Elizabeth's definition ties Woodenization to holding high standards through clear, relentless modeling; and Tim's definition reframes the whole practice as an expression of respect for students rather than mere compliance-training. Stuart closes by admitting that even as the person who coined the term and wrote the book, he's still deepening his own understanding of why and how to do Woodenization well, framing ongoing learning as part of the practice itself rather than something mastered once and finished.
points: John Wooden's original move — explicitly teaching college athletes how to put on socks and shoes — anchors Woodenization in the principle that no task is too small or obvious to teach explicitly.

Elizabeth's definition reframes 'high standards' away from a vague expectation and toward a concrete teacher responsibility: clearly and relentlessly modeling what's important so students can actually reach the standard.

Tim's definition connects Woodenization to respect rather than control — explicitly teaching students what they need to know and holding them accountable is framed as an act of honoring their life and journey.

Explicit task-teaching sends students a meta-signal beyond the task itself: 'anything I expect you to do, I will teach you how to do,' which builds trust in the teacher's care and rigor simultaneously.

Stuart's admission that he's still deepening his own understanding of Woodenization, years after coining the term and writing the book, models the same growth-oriented posture the strategy asks of students.
quotes: Woodenizing is explicitly teaching students how to successfully accomplish a task no matter how small or 'obvious' it might be.
Wooden's level of specificity in doing this sent clear signals to his students: anything I expect you to do, I will teach you how to do.
Woodenizing is holding students to high standards in everything by clearly modeling what's important, relentlessly.
Respecting the student, their life, their journey enough to explicitly teach them what they need to know and hold them accountable.
It's important for you to know that even the guy who wrote the book is still deepening his understanding of the why behind these strategies and the how of doing them well with real students.
